paragraphs: Three frosts fell on Chang’an in succession at the beginning of winter. The pagoda-tree leaves had not yet finished falling in the rear courtyard of the Secretariat when the military rolls from Hebei arrived.

Eight heavy wagons cut across the frozen ground, leaving ruts deep enough to hide a copper coin. The official escorting them rode a gray horse, its mane rimed with white. As soon as he entered the courtyard, he urged the clerks to open the chests. Pointing to the uppermost seal, he announced, “The four prefectures of Hebei report more than 281,600 men liable for service. Your Highness, please acknowledge receipt at once.”
Fu Hong was shaving old characters from a wooden tablet with a small knife. The shavings beside his inkstone looked like pale-yellow threads.
“Liable for service?” he asked.
“The figures were checked against the old district registers.”
“I asked about the men.”
The official hesitated, then smiled. “Every man is on the rolls. All four prefectures have submitted their figures, each signed by its governor and magistrates.”

Fu Hong closed the tablet and looked toward the wagons. Beneath their oilcloth coverings lay nothing but paper and bamboo slips. A few years earlier the court had pressed the provinces to put their military rolls in order, and every district had found an excuse to delay. Now, as soon as word spread that Chang’an wished to know whether a distant expedition was possible, the old registers came racing in, one faster than the next.
“Store them in the western repository. Do not break a single seal. Make another register recording who reported each figure, who copied it, and every posting station the wagons passed through.”
The official’s smile faded. “Your Highness, the gentlemen of Hebei are only eager to serve the state.”
“I know,” Fu Hong said. “We will speak of service when we can recognize every name.”

Over the next ten-odd days, rolls came in from Hexi, Guanzhong, Bingzhou, and Youzhou. On the western wall of the Secretariat, where the autumn tax assessments had once hung year after year, a new wooden board was mounted. Scores of columns had been left blank. With each delivery, a clerk filled another line in heavy ink.
Guanzhong reported 210,000, Hexi 130,000. When the old rolls from Heluo, Nanyang, Bashu, and the frontier commands were added, the grand total finally passed 1.1 million.
The number traveled through Chang’an faster than the vermilion seal on an official dispatch.

In the Western Market, drinkers tore flatbread and boasted that if all Qin’s soldiers marched, their discarded whips alone could dam the river. Smiths bought up scrap iron through the night. Horse dealers demanded the price of a fine mount for their leanest nags. Outside the eastern gate, the owner of a cart yard who had been preparing to close lifted the FOR SALE board from his door the moment he heard that the court might requisition wagons.

A fortune-teller displayed a sheet of red paper beside the imperial avenue, promising that before another year passed the southern emperor would come north to surrender. A white-haired old woman listened for half the morning before asking, “If all the realm belongs to one family, will my son be spared another year on the frontier?” The fortune-teller called her a spoilsport and drove her away.

When Fu Pi saw the wooden tally board in Chengming Hall, he was holding a newly drawn chart of the Xiangyang waterways. He had worked over it for days: the Han River, its ferry crossings, the anchorages for naval drills, all marked with fine red dots. Since the defeat along the Huai, he had questioned boatmen again and again about currents and channels. Even the exacting Fu Rong admitted that he no longer argued for war on courage alone.

“Take six hundred thousand from the million and advance on three fronts.” Fu Pi pinned the words *Jiankang* beneath his knuckles. “If the northern bank resists, our eastern army crosses the Huai first. If Jiangling sends help, our central army blocks it. The fleet goes down the Han. The Jin court will be unable to defend both ends.”
Fu Jian listened closely.
“How many will remain in the north?”
“At least four hundred thousand among the provinces, besides the district garrisons. Enough to hold it.”
“Hold what, with those four hundred thousand?”
Fu Pi ran his finger from the northern edge of the map all the way to Hexi. His hand moved quickly; passes and towns disappeared beneath a single fingertip.
Standing beside him, Fu Rong picked up the rolls and opened the Hebei section. “This list counts the men guarding Ye among those available for the southern expedition.”
“The garrison can be relieved.”
“By whom?”
Fu Pi pressed his lips together and did not answer at once. Fu Jian rolled up the map and ordered the crown prince summoned.
“Do not use the provincial totals yet. Check them for me. Every one.”

As Fu Hong accepted the order, Fu Pi looked impatiently at the thin sheet in his younger brother’s hand. He bore him no ill will. He had seen men on the walls of Xiangyang hurl stones down upon the attackers; he knew that every day an army went without reinforcements was a day its men staked their lives. A battlefield would never give him the leisure of the Secretariat to scrape every entry clean.
The first crack in the rolls appeared in Fufeng.

Zhao Wu, son of Zhao Mian, a native of Anling in Fufeng. His name appeared on the military rolls of three counties. In one he was forty-seven; in another thirty-two; in the third nineteen. All three county offices could produce a grain voucher bearing his name. Not one could bring Zhao Wu before the inspecting officer.
A county lieutenant slapped a chest in protest. “It is written here in black and white. How could it be wrong?”
Song Cheng, the inspector, laid the three tablets side by side. “Then have all three Zhao Wus report for muster tomorrow.”
The lieutenant had nothing to say.

In half a month, nearby counties uncovered more than four hundred places held by duplicate names or duplicate claims. Some men were entered in two districts and drew rations from both. Some claimed armor in a dead brother’s name. Powerful households had enrolled their tenants as soldiers; when the court came to inspect, the tenants were merely dressed in old armor and made to stand in line. The county lieutenants blamed one another. None admitted to having begun it.

Song Cheng carried the rolls back to his station and wrote his report through the night. He had been a county clerk himself. He knew how years of copied records bred such mistakes; to condemn them all as embezzlement might turn rosters left over from garrison rotations a decade earlier into evidence of killings that had never happened. Yet he had to cut somewhere, or those 1.1 million men would live forever as characters on a page.
Li Shou of Hedong, meanwhile, had been dead for three years.

When the two inspectors Song Cheng sent reached his village, melting snow had softened the wooden threshold. Li Shou’s mother was airing an old soldier’s coat outside the door. Its collar had been mended three times, the stitches growing closer with every repair. At the sight of young men in official dress, she went first to find a wooden box inside the house.
“Are you looking for Ah-Shou?”
“The military rolls say he is still serving in camp.”
Holding the box, she said nothing. At last she opened it slowly. Inside lay half a wooden muster token, a pair of shoes caked with old mud, and a letter she could not read.

“He said it rained so much along the Huai that a pair of shoes would not last him a month.” She bent her head and touched the worn edge of a shoe. “After that, other men’s horses came home. Ah-Shou did not.”
The inspector could hardly bear to question her further, but the regulations required one more thing. “How much compensation have you received?”
“Two *dou* of millet. Nothing after that. The village said he was still counted as a military household. Once the court checked his name next year, they would make up the rest.”

The inspector took out the military tablet. His vermilion brush rested beneath the words *still living* for a long time. Removing a man from the rolls took one red line; tracing three years of rations claimed in error meant searching company rolls, officers' marks, granary records, and guarantors' signatures. Watching the red brush, the old woman suddenly asked, “Once you cross him out, does his grave stop being a soldier’s grave?”
“The grave is still there,” the inspector said. “And the compensation owed to him is still owed.”

The words were out before he regretted how quickly he had promised. Back at the posting station, he added one line to the end of his report: compensate Li Shou’s family for the three unpaid years before investigating those who claimed the grain. By the time that line reached the Secretariat, two other provincial dispatches had arrived asking permission to postpone the recovery of old debts.
Fu Hong read them without anger. He merely ordered that Li Shou’s tablet be left upon his desk.

Winter gave way to spring. The ink on the Secretariat’s western wall grew denser, but its colors began to change. At first every man reported liable for service had been entered at the provinces' word. Now the rolls had to distinguish those who could leave their posts from those fit for distant campaigning. Black slips marked frontier defenders, strategic garrisons, and palace guards who could not be moved. Yellow slips marked military households farming garrison land or working with carts, boats, salt, and iron: men who could be called away briefly but not for long. Only those inspected in person, provisioned, tested on the march, and checked against the needs of the garrisons they would leave behind could be given red slips for the expedition.

Youzhou reported twelve thousand cavalry, yet fewer than eight thousand horses could survive a long march. An old beacon guard in Bingzhou was sixty-four, his hands and feet stiff from frost; kneeling on the drill field, he could not even draw his bow. Yet if he were taken away, no one else would guard the signal fire at the mountain pass. At the salt wells of Bashu, thirty thousand military households knew how to handle blades, but also how to boil salt, forge iron, and repair plank roads. Hearing of the inspection, a magistrate declared, “If the court wants men, I would not dare keep a single one.”
Fu Rong copied that sentence to Fu Hong. “Have him calculate first what salt the Qin army will eat when these men are gone and the grain must be carried south.”
The crown prince visited a farming garrison near the capital himself.

The fields were being turned that day. The soldiers had shed their armor and were washing plowshares by a little ditch. Several children searched for insects among the furrows. Seeing official riders in the distance, they fled toward the edge of the field. A young soldier-farmer recognized the crown prince and frantically tried to wipe the mud from his boots on the grass.

Fu Hong told him to go on holding the plow. Fresh calluses covered both the man’s palms. The tip of his left little finger was gone, lost at Wei Bridge some years before. He said that if a mobilization order came, he would pack tonight and leave at dawn.
“And the wheat?”
“My mother and my wife can harvest some of it.”
“How old is your mother?”
“Fifty-eight.”

Fu Hong looked toward the headland. The old woman carried a small grandson on her back. The wind lifted the gray hair at her temples. When she saw the crown prince looking, she bowed hurriedly; the child, too young to understand, waved a broken stalk of wheat in the visitor’s direction.
“If you are away for a year, what becomes of the fields?”
The soldier lowered his eyes. “If the rain comes next year, something will still grow.”
“And if you do not return?”
He laughed once, then stopped. “Your Highness, then let the little one learn a few characters. Someday he can read my army letters to his grandmother.”

Fu Hong dismounted and asked the camp commander how much millet they had harvested the year before, how much seed remained, and how many mouths depended on each military household. He did not exempt anyone from service on the spot. Days later, the fourteen hundred men of that camp, originally marked red, were marked yellow instead. Beside the entry he attached an estimate of grain production and the hands required to replace those sent away. A Secretariat official said that the crown prince pitied the common people too much and might obstruct the state’s great undertaking. Fu Hong merely told him to go and reckon the autumn harvest with the old woman again.
To find, among 1.1 million names, the men truly able to wage a distant war was far harder than conjuring a magnificent number.

Murong Chui’s method was rougher. He had no love of long hours with registers, but knew that *able-bodied soldier* was often little more than an agreeable phrase. He selected a dozen or more units from different provinces, ordered each man to shoulder fifteen days' rations, and marched them three hundred *li* with light equipment. No one was to accept extra horses or wagons offered by great households along the road.

On the first day everyone fought to be at the head of the column. On the third, men from a Hebei unit nearly drew blades over two carts of grain cakes. On the fifth, some discarded their spare bowstrings on a riverbank and could only stare helplessly at their bows during the shooting drill. On the seventh, one commander fell ill and three captains of his camp simultaneously issued different orders. A Qiang soldier slipped away alone at night to find water, then could not find his own camp gate on returning. When the exercise was over, many remained brave men. Far fewer than the provincial officials had imagined had been able to finish the march.
Fu Pi arrived to observe the review just as a military physician was washing burst blisters from several soldiers' soles with warm water.
“Do we throw a man away because his feet hurt?”

Sitting at a low desk, Murong Chui used his knife to split open a moldy wheat cake. “A man with sore feet can kill an enemy. When he finally reaches the Huai, if he cannot even draw his blade, whose life will that cost?”
“Who can promise to bring every man through a battle alive?”
“No one.” Murong Chui tossed the cake back into the basket. “But if you know ten wagonloads of food have become six, you cannot set your march by ten.”

Fu Pi crouched to look at the wounded feet. During the siege of Xiangyang, a commander burning with fever had insisted on mounting his horse; on the third night after they carried him down, he died. Fu Pi still remembered his name. He stood, told his attendants to copy the physician’s record of sick and injured men, and offered no further argument.

By early spring of the twentieth year of Jianyuan, the audit was still under way. The original red-tag list held 390,000 men. Of those, 140,000 were garrison farmers who could not be spared long during spring planting. After subtracting units that had to rotate through guard duty, replacing those who would leave empty posts, and checking roads, provisions, and relief cycles again, the force that could sustain a prolonged campaign in the south was finally reckoned at around 250,000.

The Secretariat sealed three chests. The first held troop rolls, the second grain reserves and transport costs, the third boats, carts, draft animals, and civilian laborers. Each lid bore the checking clerks' signatures. One high officer’s seal was no longer permitted to hide the mistakes of a dozen men.
Fu Jian opened the troop chest first. When he read *approximately 250,000*, his face showed little.
“And the 1.1 million?”

“There are still that many names,” Fu Hong said. “Some belong to frontier guards. Some to men killed in battle whose names were never struck off. Some draw pay though they no longer serve in camp. As for the rest, we now know who can go and who must stay.”
“If I wanted four hundred thousand?”
“They could be raised.”
Fu Pi lifted his eyes at that.

Fu Hong continued, “We would have to take another 140,000 from the farming garrisons and suspend part of the spring planting in Heluo and Guanzhong. Six to eight thousand boats; three hundred thousand oxen and horses; at least four hundred thousand civilian porters for the supply lines. If the war lasted only six months, we might barely sustain it. If it ran into another year, grain from Hexi and Bashu would have to be brought in as well.”
Fu Jian turned the page. “And if drought or flood strikes again?”
“I dare not offer Your Majesty a pleasing figure.”
“Then tell me the ugly one.”
“People will starve.”
The hall went quiet. At last Fu Pi said, “If the south can be brought under one rule soon, fewer men will die on the frontiers year after year. No war has ever come without a price.”

Fu Hong did not dispute it. His elder brother still bore scars from Xiangyang upon his shoulder. Fu Hong knew these were not words learned at a feast. He simply took a rubbing of Li Shou’s half token and laid it at one corner of the map.
“If the price must be paid, allow me first to write down who will pay it. The next grain sent as compensation must not be delivered to a living name on a register and a dead man’s door.”
Fu Jian rubbed the chest lid with his fingertips and asked Murong Chui, “Are two hundred and fifty thousand enough to take the south?”
“Enough to fight a very great battle.”
“I asked about the south.”
“I have never been to Jiankang. I cannot calculate where the men of Jin will make their last stand.”

Fu Jian looked to Fu Rong. His brother pushed the transport chest closer, speaking more gently than usual. “Your Majesty can call up more men if you choose. But you would be calling up the north’s fields and granaries, its trade routes, and the families left behind in old towns. The next edict must say who will look after them.”

Fu Jian was silent for a long time before ordering the three chests to remain in the hall. Once the ministers had withdrawn, he walked alone to the window. The board on the western wall, the one bearing *1.1 million*, was being taken down. Two clerks carried it across the wet earth. Morning sunlight fell between the corridor pillars and turned the old writing gray, layer by layer. The name Zhao Wu, once entered in three counties, had long since been scrubbed away, but the wood beneath it looked newer than the rest.
Fu Jian called after them. “Do not burn that board.”
“Does Your Majesty wish to preserve it as evidence?”
“Put it in the old repository of the Secretariat.”

The clerks carried it away at his command. On the back was blank space enough for a still greater number next year. Fu Jian suddenly remembered Wang Meng saying on his deathbed that an emperor saw a ledger, while his minister saw the dead along the roads that carried the grain. At the time he had understood only half.
That day, the rolls of two hundred and fifty thousand men lay upon the imperial desk.
They weighed no less than the 1.1 million.
